pages.title: Think Like a Researcher
pages.subtitle: A Cheat Sheet for Clear Thinking, Great Groups & Solid Stats

panels.heading: Start with the Right Questions
panels.body:
A great question is: Important (why does it matter?); Specific (not too broad); Testable (falsifiable); Feasible (with available resources); Novel (adds to knowledge).
Bad question: "Does X improve Y?" Better: "How does X affect Y under condition Z, measured by M?"

panels.heading: Think Clearly: A Framework
panels.body:
Understand the problem deeply: Read, talk to experts, observe.
Map assumptions: What do you believe to be true?
Generate hypotheses: Make predictions (directional if possible).
Design a test: How will you know you're right or wrong?
Run & collect data: Follow the plan. Be rigorous.
Analyze objectively: Let the data speak.
Interpret & contextualize: What does it mean? What are limitations?

panels.heading: Good Experiment Design
panels.body:
Control confounders: Hold other variables constant or randomize.
Randomize: Avoid order effects and bias.
Use baselines: Always compare to a strong baseline.
Pre-register (if possible): Write down your plan and analysis before seeing results.
Power analysis: Make sure your sample size can detect meaningful effects.
"The goal is not to prove you're right. The goal is to learn what's true."

panels.heading: Build & Work in Great Research Groups
panels.body:
Roles (examples): Idea person – thinks big & asks "why?"; Skeptic – challenges assumptions; Builder – implements & iterates; Analyzer – turns data into insights; Communicator – tells the story clearly.
Best practices: Psychological safety – everyone can speak up; Disagree & commit – debate ideas, unite on decisions; Clear ownership – know who does what; Document everything – decisions, code, data, results; Regular syncs – short, focused, outcome-driven.
Avoid these traps: Groupthink – challenging ideas is seen as negative; Vagueness – unclear goals, roles, or next steps; Hero culture – one person becomes a bottleneck; Poor feedback – no retrospectives, no improvement.

panels.heading: Statistical Approaches: When & What
panels.body:
Compare means – Parametric – t-test (2 groups), ANOVA (>2 groups) – when data ~ normal, similar variances.
Compare medians / ranks – Non-parametric – Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis – non-normal data or outliers.
Categorical association – Categorical tests – Chi-square test, Fisher's exact test – counts / proportions data.
Relationship between variables – Correlation – Pearson (linear), Spearman (rank) – measure strength & direction of association.
Prediction – Regression – Linear, Logistic, Ridge, Lasso, etc. – model outcome from predictors.
Estimate uncertainty – Resampling – Bootstrap, confidence intervals – small samples or complex estimators.
Always report: effect size + confidence interval + p-value (if relevant).

panels.heading: Don't Get Fooled: Common Pitfalls
panels.body:
P-hacking: Trying many things until something is significant. Fix: Pre-register, correct for multiple tests.
Confirmation bias: Seeing what you expect to see. Fix: Seek disconfirming evidence.
Small N: Too little data = noisy & unstable results. Fix: Do power analysis.
Data dredging: Exploring data without a plan. Fix: Have a plan, use a validation split.
Causation ≠ correlation: Association does not imply causation. Fix: Use experiments or quasi-experiments.
Leakage: Information from future/target leaks into features. Fix: Check data pipeline!

panels.heading: Analyze Like a Pro
panels.body:
Visualize first: Plots reveal issues fast.
Summarize simply: Mean ± SD, median [IQR], counts, rates.
Quantify uncertainty: Use CIs, not just point estimates.
Check assumptions: Normality, homoscedasticity, independence.
Sensitivity analysis: Do results hold under reasonable changes?
"Let the data speak, but you have to ask the right questions."

panels.heading: The Researcher's Mantra
panels.body: Be precise in your questions. Be rigorous in your methods. Be honest in your analysis. Be humble in your conclusions. Be useful with your findings.

pages.footer: Remember: Curiosity starts it. Discipline drives it. Skepticism improves it. Collaboration accelerates it. Good science changes the world.
pages.summary: A guide to doing research well: asking sharp, testable questions, designing fair experiments, working well in a team, picking the right statistical test, and avoiding traps like p-hacking and data leakage.

pages.title: Basic Math for Deep Learning Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Vectors, matrices, gradients, probability, and the minimum math intuition you need

panels.heading: Core Objects
panels.body:
Diagram: pipeline Input x → Linear algebra → Nonlinearity σ(·) (ReLU, tanh, …) → Loss L(y, ŷ) → Gradients ∇L → Updated weights W ← W − η∇L.
Scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors: Scalar – single number (e.g. 3.14), shape (); Vector – 1D list of numbers, shape (d,); Matrix – 2D table, shape (n × d); Tensor – n-D array, shape (b × t × d). ELI5: Containers of numbers. Why it matters: Data, activations, and weights all live in these objects.
Shapes and dimensions: B – batch size (samples in parallel); T – sequence length (time / tokens); D – feature / hidden size (embedding dim); C – channels (e.g., color channels); H – height (image rows); W – width (image cols). Example image batch shape: (B, C, H, W). Example text embeddings shape: (B, T, D). Watch out: Most bugs are shape mismatches!

panels.heading: Linear Algebra Basics
panels.body:
Dot product: x · w = Σᵢ xᵢwᵢ. ELI5: Weighted similarity / one neuron score. Use: Linear layers, attention scores, cosine-style intuition.
Matrix multiplication: Y = XW + b with shapes (n × d)(d × h) → (n × h). ELI5: Many dot products at once. Watch out: Inner dimensions must match (d here)!
Transpose & reshape: Transpose swaps axes (A → Aᵀ). Reshape (view) changes arrangement. Squeeze / unsqueeze add or remove size-1 dimensions.
Norms & distance: L1 norm ‖x‖₁ = Σ|xᵢ|; L2 norm ‖x‖₂ = √(Σxᵢ²); distance d(x, y) = ‖x − y‖₂. ELI5: "How big" or "how far". Use: Regularization, nearest neighbors, embedding similarity.

panels.heading: Calculus for Learning
panels.body:
Derivative / slope: dy/dx is slope / sensitivity (the tangent line). ELI5: How much output changes when input changes a little. Use: Understand growth, training signals, optimization.
Partial derivatives & gradient: For many variables ∂L/∂wᵢ. Gradient ∇L = [∂L/∂w₁, ∂L/∂w₂, …, ∂L/∂wₙ] points in the direction of steepest ascent. ELI5: Arrow pointing uphill fastest. Training goes the OPPOSITE direction.
Chain rule (backprop idea): If y = f(g(x)), gradients pass through both: ∂L/∂x = ∂z/∂x × ∂y/∂z × ∂L/∂y. Core idea of backpropagation! Multiply local effects along the path. Backprop = chain rule in reverse.
Gradient descent: Update rule w ← w − η∇L, where η = learning rate. Too small (very slow), just right, too big (overshoots). ELI5: Walk downhill to reduce loss. Use: Training neural networks.

panels.heading: Probability & Stats Basics
panels.body:
Mean, variance, std dev: Mean μ = (1/n)Σxᵢ; Variance σ² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ)²; Std dev σ = √σ². Use: Normalization, noisy results, uncertainty, data summaries.
Probability, expectation, sampling: P(A) = chance of event A; Expectation E[X] = Σₓ x P(x); Sampling: draw examples ~ P (from a bag/data population to a random sample). Use: Data, stochastic training, simulation, generation.
Common distributions (intuition): Bernoulli (binary) P(X=1) = p; Categorical (classes/tokens), k classes, ΣPᵢ = 1; Gaussian (continuous) N(μ, σ²). Use: Model randomness, noise, data generation, uncertainty.
Log, exp & softmax: exp turns any score → positive; softmax converts logits z to probs: pᵢ = e^zᵢ / Σⱼ e^zⱼ (sum = 1); log turns products → sums: log(ab) = log a + log b. ELI5: Softmax is a "who gets the confidence" function.

panels.heading: Losses You Meet All the Time
panels.body:
MSE (mean squared error): MSE = (1/n)Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Use: Regression (predict numbers). ELI5: Penalizes large errors more.
Cross-entropy (CE): Binary (with sigmoid) CE = −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]; Multiclass (with softmax) CE = −Σ yᵢ log pᵢ, where y is true (0/1 or one-hot) and p is predicted prob. ELI5: Punish being confident and wrong. Use: Classification (labels / classes).
Regularization: L2 (weight decay) λ‖W‖₂² = λΣw² (small & dense weights); L1 (sparsity) λ‖W‖₁ = λΣ|w| (sparse weights). Why: Reduce overfitting, control complexity, improve generalization. ELI5: Keep weights from getting too wild.

panels.heading: Quick Researcher Checklist
panels.body: 1. What are the shapes? 2. What operation is happening? Dot? Matmul? Elementwise? 3. What is the loss? 4. What quantity are we differentiating? ∇L w.r.t. what? 5. Are values normalized or exploding? 6. Are probs actually probabilities? Softmax / sigmoid? 7. Is result an average, a sum, or an expectation?

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes / Traps
panels.body: 1. Shape mismatch: (n,d)(h,k) with d ≠ h – must match! 2. Wrong operation: Matmul ≠ elementwise. 3. Forgetting bias: y = XW vs y = XW + b – bias matters! 4. Mixing logits with probs: Don't feed logits to loss expecting probs, and vice versa! 5. Vanishing / exploding gradients: too tiny or too huge. 6. Averaging over wrong dimension: Mean over batch? Over time? Be intentional! 7. Using wrong loss for the task: Classification ≠ regression.

pages.footer: First track the shapes. Then track the objective. Then track the gradient. Deep learning math = linear algebra + calculus + probability + careful thinking.
pages.summary: The minimum math behind neural networks: how data is stored as vectors, matrices and tensors, how gradients and the chain rule let a model learn by walking downhill on its loss, and the probability ideas and loss functions that show up everywhere.

pages.title: Deep Learning Basics Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Embeddings, pooling, normalization, nonlinearities, training, and core intuition

panels.heading: Core Idea
panels.body:
Diagram: pipeline Input data x → Layers (neural net) → Prediction ŷ → Loss (score) L → Backprop (gradients) ∇L → Updated weights W′.
Neuron / linear layer: y = Wx + b. ELI5: Mix inputs with weights, then add bias. Pro: Flexible building block. Watch out: Alone it only makes linear decisions.
Nonlinearity / activation: Adds bends to the model (ReLU = max(0, x), Sigmoid, Tanh). ELI5: Gives the network the power to model non-straight-line patterns. Pro: ReLU is the default workhorse. Watch out: Sigmoid/Tanh can saturate. ReLU can "die" (stuck at 0).
Loss function: Score = how wrong the model is. Classification: cross-entropy −Σ y log(ŷ). Regression: MSE (1/n)Σ(y − ŷ)². ELI5: The score that tells the model how wrong its predictions are. Pro: Guides learning. Watch out: Must match the task.
Backpropagation: Pass blame backward. ELI5: Send blame (gradients) backward so each weight learns how to change. Pro: Efficient with chain rule. Watch out: Needs a good learning rate & optimizer.

panels.heading: Representation Building Blocks
panels.body:
Embeddings: Look up dense vectors (an embedding matrix row for each token such as cat, dog, pizza, <UNK>). ELI5: A lookup table that gives each item a learned meaning-space coordinate. Use when: Discrete tokens / IDs / categories.
Convolution: Slide a filter to find patterns, producing a feature map. ELI5: A small filter scans the input looking for useful patterns. Pro: Captures local patterns. Pro: Weight sharing = fewer params.
Pooling: Downsample & summarize (max pool 2×2, avg pool 2×2). ELI5: Summarize a local region to shrink size and keep key info. Tradeoff: Loses some detail.
Batch normalization: Normalize activations (unstable before → stable after). ELI5: Stabilizes layer activations during training. Pro: Faster & more stable training. Note: Uses batch stats in training, moving averages at inference.
Dropout: Randomly drop during training. ELI5: Randomly turn off some units so model doesn't rely too much on any one path. Pro: Strong regularization. Note: Off during inference.

panels.heading: Training Basics
panels.body:
Batch / mini-batch / epoch: Batch – one update using all data. Mini-batch – update using a subset. Epoch – one full pass over the data. ELI5: Balance between speed, noise, and stability.
Gradient descent & LR: Update weights opposite the gradient: w ← w − η∇L, η = learning rate. Too small: very slow. Just right: good progress. Too big: unstable! ELI5: Step size for each update.
Optimizers: Popular choices. SGD – simple baseline + momentum. Adam – adaptive LR + momentum. ELI5: Different optimizers = different ways to choose update steps.
Overfitting vs underfitting: Look at train vs. val loss curves. Pro: Use validation curves to decide when to stop or adjust model.
Train / val / test split: Keep the exam secret. Train ~70%, Val ~15%, Test ~15%. ELI5: Train learns, Val tunes, Test is the final exam. Pro: Prevents cheating. Watch out: Never tune on test!

panels.heading: What Each Block Is Good For
panels.body: Embedding: tokens / categories. Convolution: images / local patterns. Pooling: reduce size / gain invariance. Batch norm: stabilize training. ReLU / activations: add expressive power. Dropout: reduce overfitting. Use the right tool for the right job!

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes
panels.body:
Dead ReLUs: Diagnosis – neurons stuck at 0. Fix – lower LR, use Leaky ReLU, or better init.
Vanishing / exploding gradients: Diagnosis – gradients too small or too big. Fix – gradient clipping, LayerNorm/BatchNorm, good init, sensible LR.
Overfitting: Diagnosis – great on train, poor on val/test. Fix – more data, regularize (dropout, weight decay), early stop.
Data leakage: Diagnosis – info from test leaks into train. Fix – clean splits, check pipelines, no peeking!
Bad normalization / unscaled inputs: Diagnosis – one feature dominates. Fix – normalize/standardize inputs & targets.
Tiny batch = unstable batch norm: Diagnosis – batch stats are noisy. Fix – larger batch, use GroupNorm/LayerNorm or SyncBN.

panels.heading: Quick Researcher Checklist
panels.body: 1. Did I define the task and loss correctly? 2. Are my train/val/test splits clean? 3. Did I choose the right representation (embedding/conv/etc.)? 4. Are activations and normalization sensible? 5. Is the learning rate stable? 6. Am I overfitting? 7. Do curves and metrics make sense? 8. Can a simpler baseline do this already?

pages.footer: First learn the pipeline. Then tune the blocks. Then debug the training.

pages.title: Cross-Validation Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: When to use each approach, what it estimates, and common traps

panels.heading: Why Cross-Validation?
panels.body:
ELI5: We train on part of the data, validate on held-out data, repeat the process, and average the results to estimate how well the model will generalize to new data.
Diagram: Dataset → Split → Train (on train folds) → Validate (on val fold) → Average score.
Pro: Better use of limited data. Pro: More stable than one random split. Con: Slower (more training cycles). Watch out: CV is not a substitute for a final untouched test set.

panels.heading: The Main Approaches
panels.body:
1. Holdout split: One train/val split. Use when data is large and quick iteration matters. Caution: high variance from one split.
2. K-fold CV (k=5 or 10): Rotate validation across k folds. Default for iid tabular data. Common k = 5 or 10.
3. Stratified K-fold: Preserve class proportions in each fold. Use for classification, especially imbalance. Caution: stratify labels, not leakage features.
4. Repeated K-fold: Run k-fold multiple times with different shuffles. Use when estimate is noisy. Caution: more compute.
5. LOOCV (leave-one-out): One sample left out each time. Use when dataset is tiny. Caution: very expensive and often high variance.
6. Nested CV: Inner loop for tuning (model tuning), outer loop for unbiased performance (perf. estimate). Use for model selection + honest evaluation. Caution: expensive, but clean.
7. Group K-fold: Keep all examples from the same group together. Use for patients, users, sessions, documents. Caution: never split same group across train and val.
8. Leave-one-group-out (LOGO): Each validation fold is one full group. Use when generalizing to unseen groups/sites. Caution: can be pessimistic if groups differ a lot.
9. Time-series / forward-chaining split: Train on past, validate on future. Use for temporal data, forecasting, drifting systems. Caution: never shuffle time.
10. Monte Carlo / ShuffleSplit: Repeated random train/val splits. Use for flexible repeated estimates on large-ish iid data. Caution: samples may appear in validation multiple times.
There's no one-size-fits-all split — choose what matches your data & goal!

panels.heading: When to Use Which?
panels.body:
Decision flow: Is the data time-ordered? Yes → use time-series split. Are there groups / patients / users / repeated entities? Yes → use Group K-fold or LOGO. Is it classification with imbalance? Yes → use Stratified K-fold. Is the dataset tiny? Yes → use K-fold, Repeated K-fold, or LOOCV (with caveat). Need hyperparameter tuning and honest model comparison? Yes → use Nested CV. Have lots of data and need speed? Yes → holdout split may be enough.
Side note: For many iid problems, start with Stratified 5-fold for classification or 5-fold for regression.

panels.heading: What Can Go Wrong?
panels.body:
Leakage from preprocessing: Scaling, PCA, imputation, feature selection must happen inside each training fold.
Tuning on the test set: Don't peek! It leads to optimistic, overfit results.
Duplicates / near-duplicates: Duplicates across folds inflate performance. Deduplicate or group similar items.
Group leakage: Same group in train & val = information leakage. Keep groups intact.
Shuffling temporal data: Shuffling destroys time order and leaks future information.
Imbalanced folds: Uneven class ratios across folds give unstable metrics.
Unfair model comparison: Compared across different folds? Not fair. Use the same folds for all models.
No variability reported: Mean score alone misleads. Always report mean ± std or confidence interval.

panels.heading: Good Practice Checklist
panels.body: Define the prediction target and unit of prediction. Split by the right unit (sample vs patient vs user vs time block). Keep preprocessing inside the fold pipeline. Use the same folds across model comparisons. Report metric mean and spread across folds. Keep one final untouched test set if possible. Choose metrics that match the task (e.g., AUROC/AUPRC/F1 for imbalance). Set random seeds and describe the split strategy.

panels.heading: Quick Reference Table
panels.body: Fast baseline → Holdout (quick and cheap). Default iid estimate → K-fold (stable and standard). Imbalanced classification → Stratified K-fold (preserves class ratio). Very small dataset → Repeated K-fold or LOOCV (use data efficiently). Unseen patients/users/sites → Group K-fold or LOGO (prevents leakage). Hyperparameter tuning + honest estimate → Nested CV (avoids optimistic bias). Forecasting / temporal drift → Time-series split (respects chronology).

pages.footer: Split like the real deployment. If reality is grouped or temporal, your validation should be too.

pages.title: Classification Metrics Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Your probe outputs a score. You pick a threshold to turn scores into yes/no. Metrics split into two families by whether they depend on that threshold.

panels.heading: Threshold-Free Metrics — Judge the Representation
panels.body:
AUROC: ELI5 – chance a random positive scores above a random negative. Pro: Threshold-free, balance-invariant, comparable across datasets. Con: Can look too optimistic when positives are rare. Use when: Default for research comparisons: layer sweeps, ablations, transfer. Diagram: ROC curve of TPR (recall) vs FPR, AUROC = 0.85.
AUPRC: ELI5 – similar idea, but only cares about your flagged items. Pro: More honest under heavy imbalance. Con: Baseline shifts with prevalence, so it is not comparable across datasets. Use when: Positives are rare (<5%). Diagram: precision-recall curve, AUPRC = 0.42 against a baseline equal to prevalence (example: 0.02).
TPR @ fixed FPR: ELI5 – if I can only review 1% of traffic, how much do I catch? Pro: Directly answers the deployment question. Con: Only one operating point. Use when: This is the "would this actually ship?" number. Example deployment dashboard at FPR = 1%: FPR (reviewed) 1.00%, TPR (catch rate) 72% — you review 1% of traffic and catch 72% of positives.

panels.heading: Threshold-Dependent Metrics — Judge a Deployed System
panels.body:
Accuracy: ELI5 – % you got right. Pro: Everyone understands it. Con: Misleading under imbalance — you can get 99% by always saying "no". Use when: Balanced classes, casual reporting only.
Precision: ELI5 – of the ones I flagged, how many were real? Pro: Measures false-alarm cost. Con: Ignores what you missed. Use when: False positives are expensive.
Recall (TPR): ELI5 – of the real ones, how many did I catch? Pro: Measures miss cost. Con: Ignores false alarms. Use when: Missing one is expensive.
F1: ELI5 – balance of precision and recall. Pro: One number, standard. Con: Depends on an arbitrary threshold, ignores true negatives, and depends on prevalence. Use when: Reporting a fixed, chosen operating point.
Fβ: ELI5 – F1 with a dial: beta > 1 favors recall, beta < 1 favors precision. Pro: Encodes real cost asymmetry. Con: You now have two knobs to justify. Use when: You can justify the cost ratio.
MCC: ELI5 – correlation between prediction and truth, from −1 to 1. Pro: Uses all four cells of the confusion matrix (TP, FN, FP, TN) and is robust to imbalance. Con: Less familiar to readers.

panels.heading: Decision Rule
panels.body: Comparing models / layers / methods → AUROC (+ AUPRC if imbalanced). Deciding whether to deploy → TPR @ FPR. Reporting a shipped system → precision and recall at your actual threshold, plus the threshold. Claiming the score is a probability → also report calibration (ECE or a reliability plot).

panels.heading: Two Traps
panels.body:
Trap 1: Never report a single accuracy number on imbalanced data. It's the classic way to look good while doing nothing. Example: with 10 actual positives and 9,990 negatives, predicting all negative gives accuracy = 9,990/10,000 = 99.9% — but we caught ZERO positives.
Trap 2: F1 without stating the threshold is unfalsifiable. Always publish the cutoff and how you chose it — ideally on a validation split, never on test.

pages.footer: The golden rule: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Don't just find patterns. Understand mechanisms.
pages.summary: Explains how to judge a classifier that outputs scores: threshold-free metrics like AUROC and AUPRC compare models, while precision, recall, F1 and friends describe a deployed system at a chosen cutoff — and why plain accuracy misleads when positives are rare.

pages.title: Imbalanced Class Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: How to evaluate, train, tune thresholds, and avoid traps when positives are rare.

panels.heading: Core Idea — ELI5
panels.body: One class (positives) is rare. Raw accuracy can look great while the model still misses what matters. Toy example of 1,000 cases: 990 negatives, 10 positives. Always predict negative → accuracy = 990/1000 = 99%, but catches 0 of 10 positives = 0 useful catches.

panels.heading: Why Imbalance Is Tricky
panels.body:
Accuracy trap: Majority class dominates the score. High accuracy can still be useless.
Minority gets ignored: Model can "win" by ignoring the rare class and still look great overall.
Calibration drifts: Predicted probabilities may be over/under-confident on the minority class.
Noisy estimates: Few positives = high variance. Scores bounce around a lot.
Choose metrics that reward catching rare positives!

panels.heading: Metrics That Matter (More Than Accuracy)
panels.body:
3.1 Precision = TP / (TP + FP). ELI5: Of predicted positives, how many are actually positive? Pro: Fewer false alarms. Watch out: Can look good by being overly conservative. Use when: False positives are costly.
3.2 Recall (TPR) = TP / (TP + FN). ELI5: Of actual positives, how many did we catch? Pro: Fewer misses. Watch out: Can be high with more false alarms. Use when: Missing positives is costly.
3.3 F1 score = 2 × P × R / (P + R). ELI5: Balance between precision and recall. Pro: Single number summary. Watch out: Hides trade-offs; depends on class imbalance. Use when: Want a balanced trade-off.
3.4 PR-AUC (PR curve): ELI5: Overall ability to find positives without too many false alarms. Pro: Focuses on the positive class. Watch out: Sensitive to prevalence (that's the point!). Use when: Positives are rare. Usually the most informative. Prefer over ROC-AUC when positives are rare.
3.5 Balanced accuracy = (TPR + TNR) / 2. ELI5: Average of recall on both classes. Pro: Treats classes more fairly. Watch out: Still a summary; check the details. Use when: You want a balanced view.
3.6 MCC (Matthews CC): ELI5: Correlation between predictions and truth. Pro: Works for any imbalance; uses all cells. Watch out: Harder to interpret. Use when: You want one robust score. Range: −1 (bad) to 0 (random) to 1 (perfect).
3.7 Confusion matrix (TP, FN, FP, TN): ELI5: The full picture. Pro: Shows where errors come from. Watch out: Counts hide rates — always compute rates too. Use when: Always!

panels.heading: Data-Level Tools (Resample Only Inside Training Fold!)
panels.body:
4.1 Stratified split / stratified CV: Maintain similar class proportions in each split. Pro: Unbiased evaluation. Watch out: With very few positives, use repeated CV for stability.
4.2 Random oversampling: Duplicate minority examples. Pro: Simple, effective. Watch out: Overfitting on duplicates.
4.3 Random undersampling: Remove some majority examples. Pro: Faster models. Watch out: May lose important signal.
4.4 SMOTE / synthetic oversampling: Create synthetic minority examples. Pro: Adds diversity. Watch out: Can make unrealistic points. Tune carefully.
4.5 Minority data augmentation: Domain-specific transforms (e.g., text back-translation, image flips, noise). Pro: Adds variety. Watch out: Don't distort the label or semantics.
NEVER resample before splitting. Do it ONLY inside each training fold. Leakage = fake performance.

panels.heading: Model-Level Tools
panels.body:
5.1 Class weights: Weight the minority class higher in the loss. Pro: Simple, built-in. Watch out: Too high can overcompensate. Use when: First thing to try.
5.2 Focal loss: Focus learning on hard, misclassified examples. Pro: Great for dense imbalance. Watch out: Extra hyperparameter (γ). Use when: Many easy negatives drown signal.
5.3 Threshold tuning: Pick threshold that optimizes your metric. Pro: Huge impact. Watch out: Tune on validation only. Use when: Always before deployment.
5.4 Cost-sensitive learning: Encode business costs (FN vs FP). Pro: Directly matches real-world trade-offs. Watch out: You must know/assume costs. Use when: You know the relative costs.
5.5 Anomaly detection / one-class methods: For extreme rarity when positives are <0.1%. Pro: Model "normal" only; flag deviations. Watch out: Needs known normal data. Use when: Positives are ultra-rare.

panels.heading: How to Choose What to Optimize
panels.body: False negatives costly (misses hurt) → prioritize recall / TPR. False positives costly (alarms hurt) → prioritize precision. You need ranking quality → optimize PR-AUC. Review budget / operating constraint → TPR @ fixed FPR or precision @ top-k. Positives extremely rare → anomaly detection + calibrated thresholding. You know business costs → cost-sensitive learning.

panels.heading: Good Workflow (A Practical Playbook)
panels.body: 1. Define: Define positive class & business costs. 2. Inspect: Check prevalence, leakage sources, data quality. 3. Stratify: Stratified split / stratified CV. Keep test untouched. 4. Baseline: Build simple baseline (e.g., majority or LR). 5. Pick metric: Match metric to goal & deployment constraints. 6. Improve: Try class weights + threshold tuning first. 7. Resample if needed: Use resampling / aug inside training fold only. 8. Inspect errors: Look at FP & FN. Find patterns and subgroups. 9. Calibrate: Calibrate probs (Platt / isotonic) if needed. 10. Report: Report chosen metric + CI/uncertainty. Explain trade-offs. Measure, improve, repeat!

panels.heading: Classic Traps (Avoid These!)
panels.body: Reporting accuracy alone: Looks good, means nothing. Leakage from resampling before split: Synthetic samples leak information. Balanced test set hides true prevalence: Results won't match real-world rates. Duplicates across folds / near-duplicates: Inflates performance artificially. Default 0.5 threshold without tuning: Rarely the right operating point. Perfect score on tiny support: Don't trust tiny numbers. Ignore subgroup fairness & drift: Model may fail for some groups.

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: What is the real prevalence? What error (FN or FP) is costlier? Did I stratify the split / CV? Did I resample ONLY inside training folds? Which metric matches deployment? How many positives in validation & test? Did I tune the threshold on validation only? Did I report uncertainty (CI)? Did I check subgroups & calibration?

pages.footer: Don't chase accuracy — match the metric to the real-world cost.
pages.summary: Covers what to do when the thing you care about is rare: why accuracy becomes misleading, which metrics actually reflect performance, and data- and model-level fixes like resampling, class weights and threshold tuning, plus the traps that create fake gains.

pages.title: Correlation vs Causation Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Two things moving together does NOT automatically mean one causes the other.

panels.heading: Core Ideas
panels.body:
Correlation: ELI5 – two variables change together. Pro: Great for finding patterns and hypotheses. Con: Says nothing by itself about why. Use when: Exploration, monitoring, feature screening.
Causation: ELI5 – changing X would change Y. Pro: Supports actions and decisions. Con: Harder to prove. Use when: Policies, interventions, product changes, medicine.
Key rule: Correlation ≠ causation. Why? A hidden factor may drive both. Or Y may cause X. Or it may be coincidence / time trend.

panels.heading: What Fools You?
panels.body:
Confounder: A third variable affects both X and Y. Example: ice cream ↑ and drowning ↑ because summer (Z) ↑.
Reverse causality: Maybe Y actually causes X. Example: stress and bad sleep — which comes first?
Selection / collider bias: The sample itself creates a fake pattern. Example: only looking at admitted patients or clicked users.
Time trends & coincidence: Things can rise together without a direct link. Shared seasonality or pure luck can mislead you.

panels.heading: How to Get Closer to Causality
panels.body:
Randomized experiment / A-B test: Best tool when feasible. Randomization balances hidden factors (randomly assign to A – control, or B – variant).
Observational causal tools: Use controls, matching, DAGs, fixed effects, diff-in-diff, IVs when randomization is impossible. Always state assumptions.
Temporal check: Cause must come before effect. Check timing carefully.
Robustness checks: Try alternative controls, subgroups, sensitivity tests, and placebo checks. If the story breaks easily, be skeptical.

panels.heading: How to Talk Like a Good Researcher
panels.body: Exploring data? Say: "X is associated with Y." → Making an action claim? Ask: "What design supports causality?" → Can I randomize? If yes → experiment. → If no → use a causal design + assumptions + sensitivity checks. Strong claim requires strong evidence. Avoid causal words unless the design justifies them.

panels.heading: Two Classic Traps
panels.body:
Trap 1: A huge R or beautiful scatter plot is not enough (e.g. R = 0.92). Always ask: what else could explain this?
Trap 2: Action based on observational data. If you will change a product, policy, or treatment, correlation alone is risky.

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: 1. What is the claim: association or cause? 2. Could there be a confounder? 3. Could direction be reversed? 4. Did the cause happen first? 5. What design supports the claim? 6. How robust is the result?

pages.summary: Explains why two things rising and falling together doesn't prove one causes the other, the usual culprits (hidden confounders, reversed direction, biased samples, coincidence), and how experiments and careful causal methods get closer to real cause and effect.

pages.title: Something's Off?
pages.subtitle: A Cheat Sheet for Detecting Odd Results — Good researchers don't just run models. They trust, but verify.

panels.heading: Red Flags: When Results Look Odd
panels.body:
Perfect (or near-perfect) scores: 99.9% accuracy? Check for leakage or target leakage.
Way better than baseline: Huge jump without strong reason? Double-check setup.
Way worse than expected: Worse than random? Check bugs, data mismatch, or label issues.
High variance across runs: Results change a lot with different seeds? Model may be unstable or data is small.
Train >> test gap: Model memorizing training data? Generalization problem.
Strange learning curve: Loss goes up? Flat line? Something's wrong in training or data.

panels.heading: Check Data First
panels.body:
Sanity check a few samples. Do they look correct? Check data types, ranges, and units. Missing values pattern? Too many? Train/test split random? Group leakage? Duplicates in data? Label distribution correct? Any label noise?
Golden rule: If the data is wrong, no model can be right.

panels.heading: Multicollinearity: How to Detect
panels.body:
Correlation matrix: Look for high absolute correlations (|r| > 0.8).
VIF (variance inflation factor): VIF measures how much the variance is inflated. Example: X1 1.2 fine; X2 5.8 moderate; X3 17.3 high; X4 32.1 severe; X5 2.1 fine. Rule of thumb: VIF > 5 = problem, > 10 = serious.
Condition number: High condition number indicates multicollinearity (e.g. 2.4e+04). > 1000 is usually bad.
What to do: Drop one of the correlated features. Combine features (PCA, domain knowledge). Use regularization (Ridge, Lasso). Collect more data.

panels.heading: When Scores Are Perfect (or Too High)
panels.body:
Check for data leakage: Target in features? Future info in train set? Leakage in preprocessing (scaling, encoding)?
Check evaluation leakage: Train/test overlap? Cross-validation done correctly (no leakage across folds)?
Check label leakage: Is the label accidentally in the input? Are IDs or timestamps leaking info?
Check task easiness: Is the task actually trivial? Are you predicting a proxy instead of the real target?
If it looks too good… find the leak.

panels.heading: When Scores Are Too Bad
panels.body: Bug in code (loss not decreasing)? Wrong labels or misaligned data? Learning rate wrong? Model too simple (underfitting)? Data distribution shift? Features not informative?

panels.heading: Learning Curve Diagnosis
panels.body:
Good fit: Both train & test loss go down and converge.
High variance: Large gap between train and test. Overfitting.
High bias: Both losses high and close. Underfitting.
Data / label issue or bug: Loss behaves strangely. Investigate!

panels.heading: Other Diagnostic Tools
panels.body:
Residual plots: Look for patterns. Random scatter is good.
QQ plot (regression): Points should follow the line.
Histograms: Check distribution of features & target.
Outliers: Detect with boxplot or IQR rule.
SHAP / feature importance: Do important features make sense?

panels.heading: A Systematic Debugging Flow
panels.body: 1. Reproduce: Can you reproduce the result? If not, fix randomness and seeds first. 2. Check data: Sanity check samples, splits, labels. Fix any data issues. 3. Check pipeline: Preprocessing, features, model, training loop. Check for leakage or bugs. 4. Run baselines: Compare with simple models. Is your model really better? 5. Stress test: Try different seeds, splits, assumptions. Is it stable? 6. Interpret: Understand what the model learned. Does it make sense? → Trustworthy results: Now you can believe it (carefully).

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: Data looks correct. No leakage (features, labels, time). Train/test split is proper. Baseline models checked. Cross-validation done correctly. Scores are stable across runs. Learning curves look reasonable. Feature importance makes sense. Errors analyzed. Results are reproducible. I would bet money on this result? If many boxes are unchecked, don't trust the result.

panels.heading: Mental Models to Remember
panels.body: Garbage in, garbage out: Bad data → bad models. Correlation is not causation: Look for mechanisms, not just patterns. Occam's razor: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the data. Be humble: You are wrong more often than you think. Seek disconfirming evidence: What would prove you wrong? Document everything: Future you will thank you.

pages.footer: Final word: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Be skeptical, be systematic, be scientific.
pages.summary: A guide to sanity-checking machine learning results that look too good or too bad: the warning signs, where leakage hides, how to read learning curves and spot correlated features, and a step-by-step debugging routine before you trust a number.

pages.title: Transformer Internals Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Attention math, shapes, heads, cache, positions, and residual flow

panels.heading: Attention Pipeline with Shapes
panels.body:
1. Input X: [B, T, d_model]. 2. Linear projections Q, K, V: [B, T, h, d_head], where d_model = h × d_head. 3. Scores S = QKᵀ/√d_head: [B, h, T, T]. 4. Softmax (row-wise) A = softmax(S): [B, h, T, T]. 5. Weighted sum Y = AV: [B, T, h, d_head].
B = batch size, T = sequence length, d_model = model dim, h = # heads, d_head = head dim.

panels.heading: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
panels.body:
Split heads: From Q, K, V of shape [B, T, h, d_head] into head 0 … head h−1. Each head attends with size d_head.
Per-head attention: Aᵢ = softmax(QᵢKᵢᵀ/√d_head), output AᵢVᵢ.
Concat & project: Concat heads [B, T, h, d_head] → [B, T, d_model], multiply by W_O to get output Y of shape [B, T, d_model].
Cross-token communication: Every token can attend to all previous tokens (causal) across every head. Diagram: lower-triangular attention pattern of query position vs key position.

panels.heading: MHA vs GQA vs MQA
panels.body:
Q always has h heads. K, V heads vary.
MHA (multi-head attention): KV heads = h. Highest quality, highest cost.
GQA (grouped query attention): KV heads = g (g < h); query heads share K/V within groups. Balanced quality & latency.
MQA (multi-query attention): KV heads = 1. Lowest latency, some quality tradeoff.
GQA = quality/latency compromise. Compute & memory (approx.) for KV cache & matmuls: MHA ~ O(h) | GQA ~ O(g) | MQA ~ O(1).

panels.heading: KV Cache: Store K, V per Layer
panels.body:
Prefill (process full prompt): Compute K, V for all tokens 1…T. Store in cache.
Decode (generate next token): At step T+1, compute K, V only for the new token and append to cache.
No recomputing past tokens = big speedup!

panels.heading: RoPE (Rotary Positional Embedding)
panels.body:
Rotate Q and K by position p: Q′ₚ = RoPE(Qₚ, p), K′ₚ = RoPE(Kₚ, p). Diagram: vectors rotated by different angles at p = 3 and p = 7.
Encodes relative positions. Generalizes to longer sequences. KV cache needs position continuity (keep incrementing p).
RoPE is applied before attention score: use Q′ and K′.

panels.heading: Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm
panels.body:
Pre-norm (preferred): LayerNorm → Attention → add residual, then LayerNorm → MLP → add residual. Pre-norm trains deeper more reliably.
Post-norm: Attention → add residual → LayerNorm, then MLP → add residual → LayerNorm.

panels.heading: Residual Stream: The Information Highway
panels.body:
Data flows, gets mixed, then carried forward. xₗ (residual input) → Attention (mix across tokens) → add → MLP (mix within tokens) → add → xₗ₊₁ (residual output).
The residual stream carries information across the entire network depth. Don't block it. Help it.

panels.heading: Interview Drill: Prove You Get It
panels.body:
A) Derive shapes: Given B, T, d_model, h. Q, K, V: [B, T, h, d_head] where d_head = d_model / h. Scores: [B, h, T, T]. A (softmax): [B, h, T, T]. Y per head: [B, T, h, d_head]. Y (concat): [B, T, d_model].
B) Implement stable softmax: Subtract row max for stability. Where dh = d_head.
C) Why causal mask? Prevents looking at future tokens: past & self are allowed, future is masked. Essential for autoregressive LLMs.
panels.code:
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(dh)
scores += causal_mask
A = softmax(scores)
Y = A @ V

pages.footer: Track the shapes. Then track the cache. Then explain the tradeoff.
pages.summary: A look inside the transformer: how attention turns queries, keys and values into a weighted mix of tokens, how multiple heads and head-sharing variants trade quality for speed, and how the KV cache, rotary position embeddings, normalization and the residual stream fit together.

pages.title: LLM Inference & Serving Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Memory, latency, batching, decoding, quantization, and cost

panels.heading: KV-Cache Memory
panels.body:
Formula: bytes ≈ 2 × L × B × T × H_kv × d_head × bytes_per_element, where L = layers, B = batch, T = total tokens (context + generated), H_kv = KV heads, d_head = head dim. Why the factor 2? We store both Keys and Values (K + V).
Visual example config: L = 80 layers, B = 8 requests, T = 4,096 tokens, H_kv = 8, d_head = 128, dtype = BF16 (2 bytes). bytes ≈ 2 × 80 × 8 × 4,096 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 10,737,418,240 bytes ≈ 10.7 GB (10 GiB). KV cache for this batch & context (weights not included).

panels.heading: Prefill vs Decode
panels.body:
Prefill (compute-heavy): Process the entire prompt (T_p tokens) in parallel, populating the KV cache. GPU busy with big matrix multiplies.
Decode (memory-bandwidth-bound): Generate one token at a time. One new token per step. Reads the whole KV cache each time.
Prefill = parallel & compute-bound. Decode = sequential & memory-bound.

panels.heading: TTFT, TPOT & Total Latency
panels.body:
TTFT (time to first token): Time from request start to first token being returned.
TPOT (time per output token): Average time to generate each subsequent token.
Total latency ≈ TTFT + (output_tokens × TPOT). Example: TTFT = 1.250 s, TPOT = 0.045 s, output tokens = 200 → total latency ≈ 1.250 + (200 × 0.045) = 1.250 + 9.000 = 10.250 s.
Optimize TTFT for perceived speed. Optimize TPOT for long outputs.

panels.heading: Continuous Batching
panels.body:
Requests arrive and depart between decode steps. Scheduler keeps GPU full. Diagram: requests A–D join the shared decode steps at different times, filling idle slots.
Tradeoffs: + Higher GPU utilization. + Better throughput. − Queueing delay for some requests. − Fairness vs latency balance.

panels.heading: Speculative Decoding
panels.body:
Use a small draft model to propose k tokens. Large model verifies; accept the prefix. 1. Draft model (small): propose k tokens. 2. Verifier model (large): verify in parallel. 3. Accept prefix: keep until first rejection; the next token comes from the verifier.
When it wins: High acceptance rate (many tokens accepted). Verifier can process many candidates efficiently.
When it loses: Low acceptance rate (many rejections). Verifier not batch-efficient (wasted work).
Great for long outputs. Tune draft size k for your model & traffic.

panels.heading: Quantization Comparison
panels.body:
FP8 (E4M3/E5M2): ~2× smaller memory/bandwidth vs BF16. Quality very good. Native FP8 HW required for best speed & accuracy. Growing support.
INT8 (symmetric): ~2× smaller. Quality good. Broad HW support. Simple, fast. Slightly more quality loss than FP8.
AWQ (weight-only): ~2.5–4× smaller (depends on bit-width, e.g. 4-bit, and the overhead of per-group scales). Quality very good. Activation stays FP16/BF16. Minimal accuracy loss on many models.

panels.heading: Latency ↔ Throughput ↔ Cost
panels.body:
You cannot optimize all three blindly. Latency (per request), throughput (requests/sec), cost ($/hour) — tradeoffs always exist.
Lower latency: smaller batches, faster GPUs, more replicas → ↑ cost, ↓ throughput.
Lower cost: fewer GPUs, smaller models, aggressive batching → ↑ latency, ↓ throughput.
Higher throughput: larger batches, more efficient kernels, continuous batching → ↑ latency, ↑ cost.
Choose the right point for your product & users.

panels.heading: Interview Napkin Math
panels.body:
A) Weights memory (70B model): Parameters = 70 billion, BF16 (2 bytes/param): 70,000,000,000 × 2 bytes = 140,000,000,000 bytes ≈ 140 GB.
B) KV cache can dominate long context. Assume L = 80 layers, H_kv = 8, d_head = 128, dtype = BF16 (2 bytes), B = 8 requests. Context length 4K tokens ≈ 10.7 GB; 32K ≈ 86 GB; 128K ≈ 344 GB; 256K ≈ 687 GB. At long contexts, KV cache >> model weights. Ex: 256K tokens → ~687 GB KV cache vs 140 GB weights. Check the numbers. Know where the memory really goes.

pages.footer: Prefill for speed. Cache for context. Batch for utilization.
