pages.title: Post-Training & Alignment Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: From SFT to preferences, reinforcement learning, and Constitutional AI

panels.heading: The Post-Training & Alignment Pipeline
panels.body: Pretraining: Learn general world knowledge at scale. → SFT: Supervised fine-tuning on high-quality demonstrations. → Preference data / reward model: Collect preferences & learn a reward model. → RLHF / PPO or DPO: Optimize behavior using preferences (choose method). → Safety & eval loop: Evaluate, red-team, monitor, and iterate (feeding back into earlier stages).

panels.heading: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
panels.body: Imitate high-quality demonstrations. Teaches format, style, and domain skills. Strong initialization for alignment. Not enough: can still be unhelpful, biased, or unsafe. Diagram: Prompt (instruction) → SFT model → Response (gold).

panels.heading: Reward Model (Preference Modeling)
panels.body:
Pairwise preference data: For a prompt, the labeler compares two responses (e.g., prefers A over B, or C over D).
Bradley-Terry intuition: P(A ≻ B) = e^r(A) / (e^r(A) + e^r(B)). Model predicts a scalar reward r(x). Higher reward = more preferred.
Labeler bias matters: Inconsistent labels; cultural & style bias; position bias (A vs B order); malicious or low-effort labels. → Aggregate & sanity-check.

panels.heading: RLHF with PPO
panels.body:
Optimize reward while staying close to the reference (SFT) policy.
Objective (simplified): max_θ E_{x~D, y~π_θ}[r_φ(x, y)] − β KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where r_φ(x, y) = reward model score, π_θ = policy being optimized, π_ref = reference (SFT) policy, β = KL penalty coefficient.
PPO loop: 1. Collect rollouts with π_θ_old. 2. Score with reward model r_φ. 3. Compute advantages. 4. Update policy with PPO. 5. Repeat & monitor KL.
Reward hacking is real: The model can learn to exploit the reward model instead of being truly helpful. Mitigation: Stronger reward model & evals; KL regularization; diverse prompts & red-teaming.

panels.heading: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
panels.body:
Train the policy directly from preferences — no explicit reward model. Training signal: for a prompt, a chosen (preferred) and a rejected (dispreferred) response.
DPO objective (intuition): max_θ E[log σ(β · (log π_θ(y⁺|x) − log π_θ(y⁻|x)))] − λ KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where y⁺ = chosen response, y⁻ = rejected response, π_θ = policy being optimized, β = inverse temperature, λ = KL penalty (optional).
Why DPO? Fewer moving parts. No reward model training. Often more stable & data-efficient.

panels.heading: RLAIF (AI Feedback)
panels.body:
Use AI to generate critiques or preferences at scale. AI critic / judge: consistency, explainability, criteria, rubric. Outputs: pairwise prefs, scores, critiques, rewrites. Benefits: massive scale, fast iteration, fits long-tail cases.
Caveats: Model biases amplify at scale. Overconfidence & hallucinated critique. Distribution shift in judge. Still need human audit.

panels.heading: Constitutional AI
panels.body:
Make values explicit, teach the model to critique & improve itself. Principles (constitution): Write clear, actionable principles. → Supervised critique & revision (SFT stage): Generate critiques & improved revisions. → AI feedback reinforcement (preference/RL): Optimize for helpful, harmless, honest behavior. → Transparency & oversight: Document values, report evals, invite audit.
Goal: Behave according to transparent, human-readable values. Example principles: Do not cause harm. Be honest & non-deceptive. Protect privacy & security. Be fair & impartial. Respect human autonomy.

panels.heading: At a Glance: Interview Comparison
panels.body:
What it optimizes — SFT: imitation of demonstrations. PPO/RLHF: reward (via reward model) with KL constraint to reference. DPO: preference likelihood (chosen over rejected) with optional KL to reference.
Typical data — SFT: prompt → response (gold). PPO/RLHF: prompts + model rollouts + pairwise preferences. DPO: prompts + (chosen, rejected) pairwise preferences.
Key components — SFT: dataset → model. PPO/RLHF: reward model + PPO optimizer + reference (SFT). DPO: preference pairs + policy (update) + reference (optional).
Moving parts — SFT: low. PPO/RLHF: high. DPO: medium.
Strengths — SFT: simple, stable, cheap; great initialization. PPO/RLHF: very flexible; can optimize complex objectives & constraints. DPO: simpler than RLHF; often more stable and data-efficient.
Failure modes — SFT: poor generalization; copies biases & bad patterns. PPO/RLHF: reward hacking, KL drift, fragile optimization, hard to debug. DPO: pref noise hurts; over-regularization; may underfit nuances.
Best use — SFT: teach skills, format, and basic helpfulness. PPO/RLHF: when you need fine control, constraints, or tooling integration. DPO: strong baseline for preferences with fewer components.

pages.footer: Optimize what you measure — then audit what you missed.
pages.summary: Walks through how a pretrained model is shaped into a helpful, safe assistant: supervised fine-tuning on good examples, learning from human or AI preferences via reward models with PPO or directly with DPO, and Constitutional AI's approach of training against written principles.

pages.title: Evaluating LLMs Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Build trustworthy evaluations, not leaderboard theater

panels.heading: Eval Stack: End-to-End Pipeline
panels.body:
1. Task definition: Define the user task, scope, constraints, and success criteria. → Be specific about inputs, outputs, and allowed tools.
2. Dataset: Curate high-quality examples that reflect real use. → Cover breadth, edge cases, and difficulty levels.
3. Rubric / metric: Specify what counts as correct and how to score it. → Criteria, weights, scoring rules, and tie-breakers.
4. Model runs: Run the model(s) under controlled conditions. → Temperature, top-p, max tokens, tools, seeds.
5. Analysis: Aggregate results, slice by dimension, and surface errors. → Compute metrics, confidence intervals, and ablations.
6. Human calibration: Spot-check, sanity-check, and iterate the eval. → Refine data, rubric, and configurations.

panels.heading: Benchmark Contamination
panels.body:
Train / test overlap: Same or near-duplicate examples leak into both train and test.
Memorization risk: Models may memorize popular benchmarks and appear better than they truly are.
Use fresh, private, held-out sets: Fresh – new tasks not seen online. Private – internal or curated data kept private. Held-out – created after model cutoff or training.
Check near duplicates: fuzzy match, embeddings, and paraphrase detection.

panels.heading: LLM-as-Judge Biases
panels.body:
Position bias: Prefers first or left responses. Verbosity bias: Overvalues longer, more wordy answers. Self-preference: Favors responses from its own model family. Style bias: Prefers certain tones, formats, or styles. Prompt sensitivity: Small prompt changes change preferences.
Mitigate it: Blind order swap – randomize left/right and repeat. Pairwise comparison – A vs B choices reduce scoring drift. Judge ensembles – aggregate across multiple judges. Human anchor set – calibrate against human labels.
Treat LLM judges as noisy signals — measure and calibrate.

panels.heading: Pass@k: Formula & Intuition
panels.body:
Intuition: If the chance a single try is correct is p, the chance that at least one of k independent tries is correct is 1 − (1 − p)^k.
Why it works: Fail all k tries: (1 − p)^k. So succeed at least once: 1 − (1 − p)^k.
Example: If p = 0.2 and k = 5: 1 − (1 − 0.2)^5 = 0.672. More samples → higher chance of success.
Note: Assumes independence between samples. In practice, outputs are correlated → pass@k is optimistic.

panels.heading: Calibration: Confidence vs. Accuracy
panels.body:
Reliability diagram: Accuracy plotted against confidence; ideal is on the diagonal.
Expected calibration error (ECE): Average gap between confidence and accuracy across bins. ECE = Σᵢ (|Bᵢ|/N) |accᵢ − confᵢ|. Lower is better.
Confidence vs. accuracy: A well-calibrated model's curve tracks the diagonal.
Report calibration metrics alongside task metrics.

panels.heading: Human Evaluation Design
panels.body:
Rubric: Clear criteria, examples, and scoring guide (criteria, weights, score scale).
Raters: Train raters and define quality standards (qualification, practice set, ongoing QA).
Randomized / blinded order: Randomize item order and hide model identities (hide model names, randomize, hide position).
Inter-rater agreement: Measure agreement (e.g., κ, α, %) and monitor drift (κ / α, disagreements, drift over time).
Adjudication: Resolve disagreements with a senior adjudicator (escalate rules, final decision, document reasons).
Design for fairness, consistency, and auditability.

panels.heading: Uncertainty: Quantify It
panels.body:
Report n: Always report the number of examples (n) evaluated. Bootstrap CI: Use bootstrap to estimate confidence intervals. Error bars: Show 95% CI / error bars on all metrics. Avoid false precision: Don't over-interpret tiny differences within noise.
Example accuracy with 95% CI: Model A 78% ±3.2%, Model B 73% ±3.5%, Model C 66% ±3.8%.
If CIs overlap, differences may not be meaningful.

panels.heading: Error Taxonomy: Know Your Failures
panels.body:
Capability: Model lacks the knowledge or reasoning ability (wrong math, logic errors, hallucinated facts). Fix: improve data, model, or reasoning.
Retrieval: Fails to find or use relevant information (missed docs, irrelevant context, outdated info). Fix: improve retrieval, rerank, or add better tools.
Tool-use: Uses the wrong tool or wrong arguments (bad API call, wrong params, ignored results). Fix: tool prompts, validation, better schemas.
Refusal: Over- or under-refuses when it shouldn't (unnecessary refusal, unsafe compliance, policy drift). Fix: adjust policies, safety tuning, better prompts.
Formatting: Output doesn't match the required format or schema (broken JSON, missing fields, wrong structure). Fix: stricter schemas, parsers, and post-checks.

pages.footer: Measure the user task. Randomize the judgment. Report the uncertainty.
pages.summary: How to build trustworthy tests for language models: define the task and rubric, avoid benchmark contamination, correct for the biases of LLM judges, understand pass@k and calibration, and always report uncertainty and categorize failures.

pages.title: Scaling Laws & Napkin Math Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Parameters, tokens, FLOPs, memory, and utilization

panels.heading: Chinchilla Intuition
panels.body:
Compute-optimal training balances model parameters N and training tokens D. Do not scale parameters alone.
Too many params, too little data → overfitting + wasted compute. Balanced N and D → better generalization + efficient compute.
Rule of thumb (Chinchilla scaling law): D_opt ≈ 20 N (tokens). Total compute ∝ N × D. Keep N and D in balance.

panels.heading: Training Compute (FLOPs)
panels.body:
Training compute scales as FLOPs ≈ 6ND, where N = parameters and D = training tokens.
Derivation (big picture): Forward (2) + Backward (4: 2 for activation gradients, 2 for weight gradients) ≈ 6 FLOPs per parameter per token.
Example: 7B parameters (7 × 10⁹) × 1T tokens (10¹²): FLOPs ≈ 6 × 7 × 10⁹ × 10¹² = 4.2 × 10²².
Compute is the currency. More FLOPs → lower loss (until limited by data / model).

panels.heading: Memory Accounting (Training)
panels.body:
Weights in BF16: Weights ≈ 2N bytes.
Adam optimizer, everything in BF16 (optimistic floor): weights + gradients + m (1st moment) + v (2nd moment) ≈ (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) × 2N = 8N bytes (not counting activations).
Standard mixed precision keeps FP32 master weights and FP32 moments: 2N + 2N + 4N + 4N + 4N = 16N bytes.
Order of magnitude: Training memory (persistent) ≈ 8N–16N bytes. Activations add more (depends on model, seq len, batch size). Rule of thumb: plan for 1.5× – 3× the persistent baseline.
Always check in units (bytes / GB / TB).

panels.heading: Inference: Weights vs KV Cache
panels.body:
Two main memory consumers at inference:
Model weights (static): ≈ 2N bytes (bf16).
KV cache (dynamic): ≈ 2 × L × H × S × d_h × B bytes, where L = layers, H = # attention heads, S = sequence length, d_h = head dimension, B = batch size. Grows linearly with sequence length S (and batch size B).
Which dominates? Short sequences: weights dominate. Long sequences / large batch: KV cache dominates.
Tip: For long contexts, KV cache can exceed weights.

panels.heading: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization)
panels.body:
MFU = Achieved model FLOPs / Theoretical peak FLOPs.
Why MFU falls (you never hit 100%): Bubble (pipeline flushes) – devices idle during pipeline fill/drain ↓MFU. Communication – all-reduce / all-gather costs time ↓MFU. Memory bandwidth – weights / activations not ready ↓MFU. Small batches / seq – not enough work to keep hardware busy ↓MFU.
Typical MFU: 10%–40% (good); 40%–60% (excellent on large clusters).
Measure it. Improve it. It's the cheapest speedup.

panels.heading: Back-of-the-Envelope Ladder
panels.body:
From napkin to plan.
1. Know parameters (N) → estimate weight memory (bf16): Weight GB ≈ 2N / 10⁹.
2. Know weight GB → estimate GPUs needed (memory): GPUs ≈ weight GB / usable GB per GPU.
3. Know params (N) & tokens (D) → estimate training FLOPs: FLOPs ≈ 6ND.
4. Know peak TFLOPs (system) → estimate total time (seconds): Time ≈ FLOPs / peak FLOPs ÷ MFU.
5. Know seconds → estimate wall-clock time: Hours = seconds / 3600.
Example: N = 7B, D = 1T tokens, peak = 1 PFLOP/s, MFU = 30%. 1) Weight GB ≈ 2 × 7e9 / 1e9 = 14 GB. 2) If GPU has 80 GB HBM usable → GPUs ≈ 14 / 80 → 1 GPU (weights fit). 3) FLOPs ≈ 6 × 7e9 × 1e12 = 4.2e22. 4) Time ≈ 4.2e22 / (1e15 × 0.30) ≈ 1.4e8 s ≈ 1620 days ≈ 4.4 years. 5) With more GPUs, time ∝ 1 / (#GPUs × MFU).
Update any input → recompute the rest.

panels.heading: Scaling Curves & Diminishing Returns
panels.body:
Loss improves with more compute, but with diminishing returns. Diagram: loss vs training compute (10¹⁸ to 10²⁶ FLOPs) — steep gains early, then diminishing returns; gets harder & more expensive.
Frontiers: compute-optimal frontier (more data as compute grows) vs too little data (off frontier). Move the frontier: more data, better algorithms, better architectures.
Key takeaway: Scale both N and D with compute. Blindly scaling N breaks efficiency.

panels.heading: Interview Drill: Napkin Discipline
panels.body: Before you compute, say it out loud. 1. State the goal: What are we estimating and why? 2. List assumptions: Model size, precision, seq len, batch size, MFU, peak hardware, etc. 3. Write the formula: Show your starting equation. Keep it simple. 4. Plug numbers (with units): Convert everything. Don't mix units. 5. Round sanely: 1–2 significant figures is enough. Don't fake precision. 6. Check the order of magnitude: Does the result make sense? If your napkin math is off by 100×, so is your plan. Sense > speed.

pages.footer: Write the units. State the assumptions. Check the order of magnitude.
pages.summary: Teaches quick back-of-the-envelope math for large models: how to balance model size and training data, estimate training compute, memory and run time, and why real hardware never reaches its peak speed.

pages.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Features, circuits, superposition, and causal interventions

panels.heading: Superposition: More Features Than Dimensions
panels.body:
Model representations compress many features into fewer dimensions. Features mix (superpose) and interfere. In the high-dimension feature space, many true features exist and each feature is a direction; compression (model layers) maps them into a low-dimension model space with fewer dimensions, where features add, cancel, and interfere.
Interference examples: Constructive – signals add → stronger activation. Destructive – signals cancel → weaker or zero activation. Ambiguous – harder to disentangle → mixed meaning.
Superposition makes interpretation hard — but structure still exists.

panels.heading: Sparse Autoencoders
panels.body:
Learn a feature dictionary that explains activations with a sparse set of features. Activation x (from model) → encoder (E) → sparse feature activations a (few non-zeros) → decoder (D) → reconstruction x̂ (≈ original).
Feature dictionary (learned): f₁ detects numbers, f₂ end of line, f₃ quotes, … JSON keys, fₖ names of people. Neurons (uninterpretable): n₁ … nₖ have unclear meanings.
Sparse AEs separate meaning (features) from mechanism (neurons).

panels.heading: Induction Heads: Copy from Previous Occurrence
panels.body:
Learn the pattern "A B … A" → predict "B". Example sequence of tokens: The chef cooked pasta . The chef …
The induction head copies the value from the previous occurrence of "The": query (at pos 6) → attend back (find match) → copy value "chef" (from pos 1) → predict next "chef" (at pos 7).
How it works: 1. Build query from current token. 2. Attend over previous keys. 3. Peak at best match (pos 1). 4. Read value from match.
Induction heads implement in-context learning via pattern copying.

panels.heading: Circuits: Connected Features Implement Computation
panels.body:
Computation emerges from features (or heads) working together across layers. Diagram: information flows from layer 0 (input) through features and attention heads in layers 3, 7 and 12 to the output logits.
A circuit is a path or subgraph whose activity causally affects the output.

panels.heading: Activation Patching: Test Causal Contribution
panels.body:
Replace an activation with a clean value and measure effect. Clean run (reference) gives a layer ℓ activation x_clean; corrupt run gives degraded output.
Patch experiment: In the corrupt run, replace x_corrupt with the clean value → patched activation → measure change.
Significant improvement: activation is causally useful. No improvement: activation likely not causally important (or redundant).
Patch one thing at a time. Measure the difference.

panels.heading: Activation Steering: Add a Direction
panels.body:
Add a vector during inference to steer behavior. Base activation xˡ (at layer ℓ) + steering direction d (meaningful direction) = steered activation xˡ_steered.
Effects: Shift model toward a concept or style. Increase/decrease a behavior. Useful for probing and control. (Steering strength λ ranges from −λ to +λ.)
Risks: Off-manifold behavior. Degraded reasoning. Shortcut exploitation. Unintended side effects.
Steering is powerful — use small steps and evaluate carefully.

panels.heading: Correlation vs Causation Ladder
panels.body:
Climb from observation to intervention to behavioral impact.
Observe (correlation): See a pattern in the data or model. Example: feature F correlates with output Y.
Ablate (should cause): Remove or suppress F. Does Y change? Example: zero out F and compare outputs.
Patch (local causal test): Replace F (or activation) with clean value. Example: activation patching at layer ℓ.
Intervene (causal manipulation): Actively change F or its upstream cause. Example: steering, editing, or counterfactual input.
Evaluate behavior (downstream impact): Measure real task performance. Example: accuracy, win rate, helpfulness, safety.
Higher rungs give stronger evidence of causality.

panels.heading: Interview Takeaways
panels.body:
Keep these principles front and center. Interpretability is empirical reverse engineering: we don't assume meaning — we discover it through systematic tests. Avoid anthropomorphism: features are not beliefs or intentions; they are patterns in activations. Validate out-of-distribution: check generalization, robustness, and failure modes beyond the training distribution.
Good practice checklist: Form a hypothesis. Design a clean test. Control confounders. Replicate results. Report uncertainty. Share methods & data.

pages.footer: Find a pattern. Test a cause. Verify the behavior.
pages.summary: An introduction to reverse-engineering what happens inside neural networks: how models pack many concepts into few dimensions, how sparse autoencoders pull those concepts apart, and how patching and steering experiments test whether a part of the network actually causes a behavior.

pages.title: LLM Safety & Responsible Deployment Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Defense in depth, evaluation, safe helpfulness, and response

panels.heading: System Safety Map: Know Your Surfaces
panels.body:
User experience: Clear purpose & scope. Expected use guidance. Transparency & labels. Age & audience aware.
Model behavior: Align to policies & values. Refuse unsafe requests. Be honest about limits. Robust to manipulation.
Tool permissions: Define tools & actions. Least privilege access. Confirm consequential actions. Isolate side effects.
Private data: Minimize collection. Protect in transit & at rest. No unexpected sharing. Respect user rights.
Monitoring & telemetry: Observe key signals. Detect abuse & drift. Track performance. Alert & investigate.

panels.heading: Instruction Hierarchy
panels.body:
Trusted system rules override untrusted external content. From higher to lower trust: System rules – non-negotiable policies & safety guardrails. Developer intent – goals, constraints, and tool design. Configuration – model settings, tool specs, prompts. User input – real user requests & context. External content – web pages, files, third-party text.
When in conflict, higher layers win.

panels.heading: Safe Handling of External Text
panels.body:
Treat it as data: Assume all external content may be wrong, outdated, or malicious.
Isolate tools: Separate the model from execution environments and external systems.
Least privilege: Grant only the minimum permissions needed for each task.
Confirm consequential actions: Require explicit confirmation for actions that change data, spend money, or affect users.
Validate output: Check for safety, policy, privacy, and accuracy before displaying or acting.

panels.heading: Assurance Loop: Test, Learn, Improve
panels.body:
1. Define safety rubric: Set clear goals, criteria, and risk priorities. 2. Test broad scenarios: Cover diverse users, tasks, domains, and edge cases. 3. Review results: Analyze failures, near-misses, and drift. 4. Improve safeguards: Update prompts, controls, tools, and policies. 5. Rerun regression suite: Verify fixes and check for new or regressed issues. Then loop back.
Continuous assurance — ship with confidence, stay vigilant.

panels.heading: Helpfulness / Refusal Balance
panels.body:
Be helpful & safe: Provide accurate, high-quality help within the boundaries. Offer safer alternatives or lower-risk approaches. Clarify intent and assumptions.
Refuse when needed: Refuse when requests are unsafe, wrong, or out of scope. Be clear, respectful, and consistent. Provide a safe alternative or redirect when possible.
Aim for the right balance: helpful, honest, and safe.

panels.heading: Defense Layers: Stack Protections
panels.body:
Sandboxing: Isolate code execution. No network by default. Restrict files and processes.
Allowlisted tools: Only approved tools run. Validate inputs & outputs. Monitor usage.
Rate limits & quotas: Limit speed and volume. Prevent abuse and overload. Protect shared resources.
Audit logs: Log key events and decisions. Tamper-evident storage. Enable audit & forensics.
Human escalation: Escalate high-risk or ambiguous cases. Human-in-the-loop for critical actions. Clear pathways and playbooks.
Multiple layers make failure less likely and impact smaller.

panels.heading: Capability-Based Safety
panels.body:
Stronger capabilities require stronger evaluations and safeguards. Low capability: narrow tasks, limited autonomy, lower risk. High capability: broad knowledge, greater autonomy, higher risk.
As capability grows, so must: evaluation coverage + red teaming depth + guardrail strength + human oversight.
Never outpace your evaluations.

panels.heading: Incident Response: Prepare, Act, Improve
panels.body:
1. Detect: Monitor for anomalies, policy violations, and user reports. Early signal, early action. 2. Triage: Assess severity, scope, and potential impact. Understand before escalating. 3. Contain: Take steps to stop or limit harm. Disable, throttle, or isolate as needed. 4. Learn: Analyze root causes and contributing factors. Document what happened. 5. Update tests: Add tests, improve controls, and update runbooks. Prevent repeats, not just respond.
Be prepared: Clear roles & contacts. Communication plan. Runbooks & playbooks. Post-incident review. Share lessons internally.
Respond quickly. Communicate clearly. Learn continuously.

pages.footer: Build defenses around the whole system — not just the chat box.
pages.summary: Describes how to deploy a language model responsibly by protecting the whole system: ranking whose instructions to trust, treating outside text as untrusted data, stacking defenses like sandboxing and audit logs, balancing helpfulness with refusals, and having an incident response plan.

pages.title: Distributed Training Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Parallelism, sharding, memory, communication, and OOM debugging

panels.heading: Data Parallelism
panels.body:
Replicate model, split batch, all-reduce gradients. Each GPU holds a model replica, processes its own batch shard (forward + backward), then gradients are all-reduced across GPUs.
+ Simple to use and scale. + Great hardware utilization. − Full model memory on each GPU. − Comm cost grows with model size.

panels.heading: Tensor Parallelism
panels.body:
Split matrices within layer, all-gather / all-reduce. Example: linear layer Y = XW + b with W split by columns (W₀…W₃) across GPUs; each produces a partial output (Y₀…Y₃), combined by all-reduce (sum) into output Y.
+ Handles very wide layers. + Less memory per GPU. − High bandwidth required. − Needs fast all-reduce.

panels.heading: Pipeline Parallelism
panels.body:
Split layers into stages, stream microbatches. Example: stage 0 (L0–L3), stage 1 (L4–L7), stage 2 (L8–L11), stage 3 (L12–L15); microbatches μ0…μ5 flow through a pipeline schedule with forward, backward and bubble (idle) slots.
+ Handles very deep models. + Low memory per stage. − Pipeline bubbles reduce util. − Sensitive to imbalance.

panels.heading: FSDP / ZeRO
panels.body:
Shard optimizer, gradients, and parameters across GPUs in a data parallel group (FSDP full shard). All-gather (before fwd); all-reduce / reduce-scatter (after bwd).
+ Massive memory savings. + Scales to very large models. − More communication. − Complexity / tuning.

panels.heading: Mixed Precision
panels.body:
Use lower precision for compute, higher for stability. Typical dtype flow: FP32 weights (master) → BF16/FP16 weights (model) → BF16/FP16 activations → FP32 gradients (accumulate) → FP32 optimizer update.
Why it works: Lower memory. Higher throughput. Similar accuracy with scaling.
Recommended: bf16 on Ampere+. fp16 on Volta/Turing (with loss scaling). Keep layernorm, softmax in fp32.

panels.heading: Gradient Checkpointing
panels.body:
Store fewer activations, recompute during backward. Without checkpointing: many activations saved (high memory). With checkpointing: fewer activations saved (low memory); recompute segments during backward.
+ Big memory savings. + Enables bigger models/batches. − Extra compute (10–30% typically). − Best to combine with FSDP/ZeRO.

panels.heading: Communication Primitives at a Glance
panels.body:
All-reduce: Sum (or avg) across all ranks; output same as input; used for DP gradients, tensor parallel.
All-gather: Gather from all ranks; output concatenates all inputs; used for TP forward, FSDP params.
Reduce-scatter: Sum then scatter; sharded output; used for DP backward, ZeRO grads.
Broadcast: Send from root to all ranks; same as root; used for params sync, initialization.
P2P send/recv: Point-to-point transfer; custom shape; used for pipeline, topology.
Tip: Overlap communication with compute (use async ops and streams).

panels.heading: Where OOMs Come From (and How to Fix Them)
panels.body:
Weights: Model parameters (incl. buffers); grows with model size. Symptom: OOM even at tiny batch; occurs in forward start. Fix: Use FSDP/ZeRO (shard params), mixed precision (bf16/fp16), or a smaller model.
Optimizer states: States like m, v for Adam/AdamW; grows with model size × #states (AdamW ≈ 8× params in fp32). Symptom: OOM when optimizer step starts. Fix: Use ZeRO/FSDP to shard states, 8-bit optimizers (e.g., 8-bit Adam), or Adafactor / Lion.
Gradients: Parameter gradients; grows with model size. Symptom: OOM in backward near the end. Fix: ZeRO (shard grads), gradient accumulation, mixed precision.
Activations: Intermediate activations saved for backward; grows with batch size × seq len × model depth × hidden size. Symptom: OOM during forward or early backward. Fix: Gradient checkpointing, reduce batch / sequence length, activation offloading.
KV cache: Key/value cache for attention (inference); grows with seq len × layers × heads × head dim (∝ context length). Symptom: OOM at long context (inference). Fix: Reduce max context / sliding window, paged KV cache, quantize KV cache (e.g., 8-bit).
General tools: torch.cuda.memory_summary(), nvidia-smi dmon, PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True, profile memory per stage.
Rule of thumb: If it's saved for backward or lives across steps, it costs memory.

panels.heading: OOM / Training Issues: Debug Tree
panels.body:
A. Forward OOM? Likely activations (or KV). Raise at forward or early backward? Yes → likely activations (or KV cache in inference): reduce batch size, reduce sequence length, gradient checkpointing, activation offloading, mixed precision.
B. Backward OOM? Likely gradients / optimizer. Raises near end of backward or at step? Yes → likely gradients or optimizer states: use FSDP/ZeRO, gradient accumulation, 8-bit optimizer / Adafactor, mixed precision.
C. Only at long context? Likely activations / KV cache. OOM increases with sequence length? Yes → likely activations or KV cache: reduce max context, use sliding window, paged / quantized KV cache, FlashAttention / xFormers.
D. Slow / stalling? Likely communication. Low GPU utilization? High idle time? Yes → likely communication or topology: use faster interconnect, overlap comm & compute, tune collectives / bucket size, check NCCL topology. No → look elsewhere (profile compute, IO, dataloaders).
Quick checklist before you blame memory: Batch too big? Seq len too long? Mixed precision on? Grad checkpointing? FSDP/ZeRO on? 8-bit optimizer? NCCL debug info?

pages.footer: Shard what persists. Checkpoint what recomputes. Profile what stalls.
pages.summary: Explains how big models are trained across many GPUs by splitting the data, the layers, or the weight matrices, how sharding, mixed precision and checkpointing save memory, and how to track down out-of-memory errors and slowdowns.

pages.title: Tokenization Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: How text becomes IDs — and why boundaries create bugs

panels.heading: The Tokenization Pipeline
panels.body:
Text (raw), e.g. "Hello, world! How are you? Café prices: $3.50" → Normalization: Unicode normalize (NFC), case rules (model-specific), strip/replace control chars, add model-specific spaces → Segment into pieces (BPE / SentencePiece), e.g. Hello | , | world | ! → Token IDs (integers), e.g. 15496, 11, 6893, 0 → Embeddings (vectors).
Pieces are vocabulary items. IDs are what the model actually reads. Embeddings turn IDs into meaning.

panels.heading: BPE: Merges Frequent Pairs into Subwords
panels.body:
Learns merges from training text to build a vocabulary. Split into chars + special space token (low → l o w; lowest → l o w e s t; newer → n e w e r; lower → _ l o w e r). Frequent pairs get merged step by step (l o → lo; lo w → low; low e → lowe; lowe r → lower …). Resulting subword vocab: low, lower, lowest, new, newer, …
BPE is data-driven and language-agnostic. No concept of "word" — only statistics.

panels.heading: SentencePiece: Models Raw Text (Including Spaces)
panels.body:
Uses a unigram language model (or BPE variant) over raw characters. Raw input kept as-is ("Hello", " Hello", "Hello,", " Hello,"). Learn units (pieces) such as ▁Hello, ello, lo, he. Encode by choosing the most probable segmentation (unigram model: Viterbi search; BPE variant: apply the learned merges): "Hello" → ▁Hello; " Hello" → ▁ + Hello; "Hello," → ▁Hello + ,.
SentencePiece treats spaces as part of the text. Great for multilingual and code.
Vocab & special tokens — typical special tokens: <pad> padding; <bos> beginning of sequence; <eos> end of sequence; <unk> unknown token; <mask> mask (for MLM); <sep> separator. Models reserve these IDs. Don't use them as content.

panels.heading: Boundary Surprises (Where Bugs Come From)
panels.body:
Leading spaces: "cat" → [3797] but " cat" → [220] [3797]. That tiny space = an extra token.
Punctuation: "word" → [1700]; "word!" → [1700] [0]. Punct often splits off into its own piece.
Whitespace: "a b" → 4 IDs; "a    b" → more IDs. Multiple spaces = multiple tokens.
Unicode surprises: "é" (composed) → [978]; "e\u0301" (e + combining) → [68] [54939]. Visually same, tokenized differently.
Code & symbols: "x == y" vs "x===y" tokenize differently. Tokenizer may prefer longer symbol tokens.
Numbers: "12345" → 123 | 45; "12,345.00" → 12 | , | 345 | . | 00. Numbers split in non-obvious ways.

panels.heading: Token Count ≠ Word Count
panels.body:
English example: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog." Words: 9. Tokens (GPT-4o tokenizer): 9.
Multilingual differences: Japanese 日本語は美しい。 – 12 tokens; Chinese 机器学习很有趣。 – 10 tokens; Korean 오늘 날씨가 좋아요. – 11 tokens; Arabic اللغة العربية جميلة. – 9 tokens (word counts N/A). Same idea, different token counts across languages!
Why more tokens cost more: Context window fills up faster. Latency – more tokens → more compute. Cost – billed per 1K tokens. KV cache memory – more tokens → more cache.

panels.heading: Tokenizer & Model Are Coupled
panels.body:
A model expects a specific tokenizer + special tokens + template. User text → tokenizer → model.
Chat templates matter: System / user / assistant roles get wrapped with special tokens.
Mismatches cause bugs: Wrong tokenizer → garbage IDs. Wrong template → wrong behavior. Missing special tokens → truncation. Stripped spaces → different meaning.

panels.heading: Debugging Checklist
panels.body:
1. Inspect IDs & pieces: Print token IDs and decoded pieces (e.g. text " Hello, world!" → IDs [220] [15496] [11] [6893] [0]). Look for unexpected splits.
2. Test normalization: Normalize the same way the tokenizer does. NFC/NFKC, spaces, control chars, case rules. "Café" vs "Café" → different IDs?
3. Count tokens early: Count before hitting limits (e.g. input tokens 1,842 + output max 1,024 within a total limit of 4,096, buffer 200 — OK).
4. Try variants: Leading spaces? Punctuation? Newlines? Try small edits to isolate boundary issues.
5. Read the tokenizer docs: Know the model's vocab size, special tokens, and quirks. Check special tokens list, chat template, normalization rules, example encodings.

pages.footer: If the model acts weird, inspect the tokens — not just the string.
pages.summary: Shows how text is chopped into tokens and turned into the numbers a language model reads, how methods like BPE and SentencePiece build their vocabularies, and why spaces, punctuation, Unicode, numbers and other languages produce surprising token splits and costs.

pages.title: Agents & Tool Use Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: The loop, context, retrieval, and reliable actions

panels.heading: Agent Loop
panels.body:
A simple loop that works. 1. Observe: Gather inputs & signals. 2. Plan: Decide next step & tools. 3. Act / tool call: Execute action or call a tool. 4. Validate: Check results & constraints. 5. Update state: Persist new facts & outcomes. 6. Repeat: Loop until goal or stop.
Tip: Make each step observable, testable, and replayable.

panels.heading: Tool-Call Failure Modes
panels.body:
Expect failure. Detect fast. Handle cleanly.
Invalid schema: Payload doesn't match tool's schema. Fix: Validate before sending.
Permission denied: Tool or resource access blocked. Fix: Check scopes & permissions.
Wrong arguments: Types, formats, or values are incorrect. Fix: Strong schemas + argument checks.
Partial result: Tool returns incomplete or partial data. Fix: Detect & request missing pieces.
Stale state: World changed since plan was made. Fix: Re-read state. Re-plan if needed.
Timeout: Tool takes too long or doesn't respond. Fix: Set timeouts, retry with backoff.
Watch out: Don't assume success — verify every result.

panels.heading: Reliability Patterns
panels.body:
Make actions safe, predictable, and recoverable.
Typed schemas: Use strict, versioned schemas for all tools.
Tool descriptions: Clear purpose, inputs, outputs, side effects, and examples.
Validation: Validate inputs before call. Validate outputs after call.
Idempotency: Design tools to be safe to retry without causing duplicates.
Retries with limits: Exponential backoff, jitter, and a max retry count. Fail fast after limits.
User confirmation for consequential actions: Ask before irreversible, costly, or sensitive actions.
Default: Safe by design. Clear errors. Easy recovery.

panels.heading: Context Engineering
panels.body:
Keep context small, relevant, and fresh.
Hierarchy: System > Goals > Policies > Recent State > Details.
Concise state: Summarize. Keep only what's needed for the next step.
Relevant facts: Include high-signal facts and decisions that matter now.
Discard stale context: Drop outdated details, superseded plans, and noise.
Less noise. More signal. Better decisions.

panels.heading: Lost-in-the-Middle
panels.body:
Key evidence can be missed in long context: information at the start and end of a long context window is used well, while the middle is often missed.
Mitigate it: Structure – put key info near the beginning and end. Retrieval – fetch only what's relevant. Recency – keep latest facts at the end. Summaries – summarize earlier context.
Make important things hard to miss.

panels.heading: Prompt Caching
panels.body:
Reuse long, stable prefixes to save cost and time. A long stable prefix is cached; only the variable suffix changes.
Lower cost: Cached tokens are cheaper. Lower latency: Faster responses with fewer tokens. Higher throughput: Serve more requests with same budget.
Cache what changes slowly. Vary what changes often.

panels.heading: RAG Flow
panels.body:
Retrieve the right info, then answer with confidence. 1. Ingest: Collect documents from sources. 2. Chunk: Split into small, coherent chunks. 3. Embed: Convert chunks into vectors. 4. Retrieve: Find top-k relevant chunks. 5. Rerank: Reorder by relevance. 6. Answer: Generate answer with citations.
Feedback loop: Log misses, refine chunks, improve retriever.
Best practices: Clean, high-quality data. Meaningful chunking. Good embeddings. Hybrid search (BM25 + dense). Citations for trust. Evaluate & iterate.

panels.heading: When Not to RAG
panels.body:
RAG isn't always the right tool.
Needs reasoning or action: Task requires planning, calculation, tool use, or multi-step actions — not document lookup. Use: Agent loop & tools.
Corpus is weak: Low quality, sparse, outdated, or noisy data will mislead the model. Use: Improve data or don't RAG.
Latency budget is tiny: Retrieval + reranking adds latency you can't afford. Use: Smaller context or caching.
Facts already in context: The needed info is already present and reliable. Use: Answer directly from context.

pages.footer: Make actions explicit. Validate results. Keep context useful.
pages.summary: Explains how AI agents work as an observe-plan-act-check loop, how tool calls fail and how to make them reliable, how to manage what goes into the model's context, and when retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps or doesn't.

pages.title: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Choose the smallest intervention that solves the problem

panels.heading: Decision Tree: Pick the Smallest Intervention
panels.body:
Need current or private knowledge? Yes → use RAG: retrieve the facts at answer time. No ↓
Need stable behavior, style or format? Yes → start with prompting: use examples, rubrics & structured output. Still not stable at scale? Then fine-tune. No ↓
Need tool/action reliability or side effects? Yes → schemas & evals first: define tools, guardrails, and evaluations. No ↓
A well-crafted prompt is enough. Ship it.

panels.heading: Prompting (Fastest & Cheapest)
panels.body:
What it is: Steer the model with instructions, examples, rubrics, and constraints.
How to do it: Clear goal & role. Few-shot examples. Rubrics & acceptance criteria. Structured output (JSON/CSV/MD).
Good for: New tasks, prototypes, varied topics, whenever examples generalize.
Downside: Brittle at scale. Prompts drift, break with edge cases, and require ongoing handholding.

panels.heading: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
panels.body:
What it is: Grounds answers in your data at runtime. Keeps knowledge current and citeable.
How it works: 1. Retrieve → top-k relevant chunks. 2. Rerank → improve relevance. 3. Generate → answer with sources.
Needs to succeed: High-quality sources. Smart chunking. Reranking for accuracy. Citations in output. Evaluation that matches real use.
Key idea: The model writes. Your data proves.

panels.heading: Fine-Tuning (Teach the Behavior)
panels.body:
What it is: Updates model weights so the behavior becomes the default.
Good for: Repeated behavior. Specific style / tone. Domain patterns & formats.
Important: Does NOT magically add new facts. It bakes in patterns, not live knowledge.
Use when prompts aren't enough: Many edge cases to handle. Strict formats always. Consistent style & tone. Lower variance you can trust.

panels.heading: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
panels.body:
Frozen base model + trainable LoRA adapters A (d×r) and B (r×d) → updated behavior (weights unchanged except adapters).
Train small adapter matrices. Lower VRAM & compute. Cheaper training. Easy to swap & version.

panels.heading: QLoRA (Quantized + LoRA)
panels.body:
Quantized base model (4-bit) + trainable LoRA adapters A (d×r) and B (r×d) → updated behavior (economical & adapter-efficient).
4-bit base model (QLoRA). Much lower VRAM. Lowest cost experimentation. Great for many variants.

panels.heading: Economics at a Glance
panels.body:
Prompting: data prep low (write examples); training cost none (prompt only); serving cost low (context tokens); iteration speed very fast (minutes).
RAG: data prep medium-high (ingest, chunk, index); training cost none (index build only); serving cost medium (retrieval + context); iteration speed fast (hours–days).
LoRA: data prep medium (format, clean, label); training cost medium (GPU training); serving cost low (same as base model); iteration speed medium (days).
QLoRA: data prep medium (format, clean, label); training cost low–medium (4-bit training); serving cost low (same as base model); iteration speed fast (days).

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes (Watch for These)
panels.body:
Bad data amplifies: Garbage in, garbage out. Biased, outdated, or noisy data becomes confident answers. Fix: Curate, dedupe, verify, version.
Retrieval can mislead: Wrong chunks look plausible. Over-retrieval adds noise. Fix: Better chunking, rerank, filters, and citations.
Overfit formats: Model parrots training formats. Loses generalization & creativity. Fix: Diverse data, holdout evals, and regularization.
Missing evals = blind: Looks good in demos, fails in prod. No metrics, no guardrails. Fix: Define evals, automate tests, and track regressions.

pages.footer: Start with prompts. Add retrieval for knowledge. Fine-tune for repeated behavior.
pages.summary: Helps decide how to customize a language model: start with a good prompt, add retrieval (RAG) when it needs fresh or private facts, and fine-tune (cheaply, with LoRA or QLoRA) only when you need a behavior baked in — with the costs and pitfalls of each.

pages.title: Design a Support Agent for 10M Users
pages.subtitle: An LLM product-system design interview cheat sheet

panels.heading: Requirements
panels.body:
Channels: Web, mobile, in-app, email, WhatsApp, social DMs, voice.
Languages: Top 10+ languages day-1. Auto-detect & locale aware.
Latency / SLA: P50 < 2.5s, P95 < 5s, P99 < 8s. SLA: 99.9% monthly availability.
Escalation: Seamless handoff to human. Context, intent & steps preserved.
Privacy: Data minimization, encryption, GDPR/CCPA, regional residency.
Success metrics: Containment rate, resolution quality, escalation rate, CSAT, cost/resolved, safety incidents.

panels.heading: Architecture Overview
panels.body: User (any channel) → Gateway (AuthN, rate limit, WAF, geo, quota, request shaping) → Policy / router (intent classify, risk score, A/B, guardrails) → Retrieval & account APIs (vector + hybrid search, KB, account APIs, transactions) → LLM / tool executor (LLM reasoning, tools, actions, side-effects, validations) → Response builder (compose, cite, format, tone, localize) → Observability (logs, traces, metrics, alerts, dashboards, SLOs) → Evaluation (quality, safety, factuality, cost, human review) → Feedback loop (user feedback, outcomes, model & KB improvement), feeding back into the router.

panels.heading: Routing & Flows
panels.body:
Simple FAQ (low risk): User question → auto-answer from KB → resolved.
Authenticated account flow: User (auth) → tools & account APIs: verify access → fetch data → action → confirm.
High risk / complex: User issue → risky / low confidence → escalate to human with full context (telemetry, summary, suggested reply).

panels.heading: Knowledge System
panels.body:
Source & ownership: Docs, policies, help center, product data, community, logs. Owner, freshness SLA, sensitivity.
Ingestion: Connectors, crawl / APIs, change data capture, schema mapping, dedupe.
Chunking & indexing: Semantic chunking, metadata, ACLs, embeddings, hybrid (BM25 + vector) index.
Retrieval & reranking: Query rewrite, filters, hybrid search, cross-encoder rerank, diversity, MMR.
Citations: Inline citations with source title, section, and link.
Freshness: Recency boost, expiry rules, staleness alerts, re-index jobs.
Accurate • Current • Authorized • Access controlled.

panels.heading: Reliability & Tooling
panels.body:
Typed tools: Strong schemas, I/O validation, idempotent side-effects.
Permission checks: AuthZ for every tool call, scoped tokens.
Retries & timeouts: Exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breakers.
Fallbacks: Cache → smaller model → template → human.
Human handoff: Context pack: intent, steps, KB hits, actions, transcripts.
Execution flow: Plan → Validate → Authorize → Execute → Observe.

panels.heading: Safety & Privacy
panels.body:
Data minimization: Collect only what's needed. Avoid storing content longer than necessary.
Access control: RBAC/ABAC, least privilege, service accounts.
PII handling: Detect, redact, mask. Tokenize where needed. No PII in prompts/logs.
Encryption: In transit (TLS) & at rest. Key rotation & KMS.
Audit logs: Who/what/when/why. Immutable, searchable, retention policies.
Guardrails: Content safety filters. PII & secrets protection. Prompt injection defense. Tool misuse prevention. Rate & abuse protection.
Data flow: User input → redact / mask → process (LLM + tools) → response; logs contain no PII.
Privacy by design. Trust by default.

panels.heading: Scale & Cost Optimization
panels.body:
Caching: Response cache, embedding cache, KB result cache, negative cache.
Batching: Embed batches, rerank batches, tool call batches, log batching.
Model routing: Small model for easy intents, larger for complex, reasoning only when needed.
Rate limits: Per user / IP / org, burst + sustained, adaptive limits, priority tiers.
Capacity planning: Autoscale, multi-region active, queue & shed, cost budgets & alerts.
Cost controls: Token budgets by intent. Early exit / stop sequences. Context window mgmt. Compress & summarize. Right-size inference.

panels.heading: Metrics Dashboard
panels.body:
Containment rate: 68% resolved by agent. Resolution quality: 4.6 / 5 human rated. Latency (P95): 3.2s (target < 5s). Cost / resolved case: $0.21 (7-day trend). Escalation rate: 7.8% (target < 10%). CSAT: 4.4 / 5 from survey. Safety incidents: 2 (7-day trend). Volume (daily): 1.8M messages / day.
SLI / SLOs: Availability 99.9% • Error rate < 0.5% • P95 latency < 5s.

panels.heading: Rollout & Continuous Improvement
panels.body:
1. Offline eval: Test sets. Evals: quality, safety, tools. Red team. Bias & toxicity. Benchmark cost.
2. Shadow mode: Live traffic mirrored. No user impact. Compare with current system. Collect diffs.
3. Limited launch: Small % of users. Feature flags. Guardrails on. Tight monitoring. Fast rollback.
4. A/B test: Compare variants. Stat sig results. Cost & quality. Segment analysis. Pick the winner.
5. Monitor: SLOs & alerts. Drill-down. Anomaly detect. User feedback. Daily reviews.
6. Iterate: Fix issues. Improve KB. Tune prompts. Retrain / fine-tune. Ship improvements.
Measure → Learn → Improve → Repeat.

pages.footer: Design for the user journey, then earn reliability at scale.
pages.summary: A worked system-design example for an AI customer-support agent serving 10 million users: requirements, the end-to-end architecture, routing by risk, the knowledge base, reliable tool calls, privacy safeguards, cost control, the metrics to watch, and a safe step-by-step rollout.
